summary: Defines internationalized domain names and the IDNA mechanism, which lets domain names use non-ASCII characters from Unicode while representing them using ASCII so existing DNS software keeps working. It was replaced by RFC 5890 and RFC 5891.

plainLanguage.summary: IDNA lets a web browser or mail program work with a domain name written in letters other than the 128 ASCII characters. The application converts the name into an ASCII form before handing it to the DNS, and converts it back before showing it to the user. Nothing else in the network has to change: the DNS servers and resolvers still see ordinary ASCII names.

questions: what does xn-- mean in a domain name
how do internationalized domain names work
subtitle: A way for applications to use non-ASCII domain names without changing DNS, resolvers or servers.

tldr.problem: Domain names could only use the 128 ASCII characters, so a name in another script had no standard way to exist. Earlier proposals for internationalized domain names needed new DNS servers, new resolvers and new applications, all at once.
tldr.mechanism: IDNA defines two conversions an application performs on each label. ToASCII runs Nameprep and Punycode to build an ASCII label that starts with the prefix xn--, and ToUnicode reverses it for display. The DNS, the resolvers and the servers keep seeing plain ASCII and need no change.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3490 was a Proposed Standard from March 2003 and has been obsoleted by RFC 5890 and RFC 5891, which split the rules into a protocol document and a separate definition of the allowed characters.

facts.label: Failure behaviour
facts.value: ToASCII can fail; ToUnicode never fails

today: RFC 3490 is a Proposed Standard from March 2003, and it has been obsoleted by RFC 5890 and RFC 5891, which split the mechanism and the rules about which characters are allowed into two separate documents. The RFC itself notes that IANA assigned the ACE prefix in consultation with the IESG.

sections.title: The Problem IDNA Solves
sections.content:
Until this RFC there was no standard way for a domain name to use characters outside ASCII. The RFC's answer is to define internationalized domain names, which use the Unicode repertoire with some restrictions, and a mechanism for handling them.

The design decision that matters is where the work happens. IDNA lives entirely inside applications. It is not a client-server protocol and needs no negotiation. The alternative proposals that came before it depended on updating user applications, resolver libraries and DNS servers at the same time, so a user could not use an internationalized name until every part of the system had been changed. IDNA requires only that the application changes: the ASCII name service already provided by the DNS is enough.

The RFC is careful about what IDNA does not do. It does not change the service DNS offers applications, which is still an exact-match lookup: either the name matches a record or it does not. It does not solve the linguistic problems of typing names in different scripts. A name written with a mix of traditional and simplified Chinese characters does not map to a single canonical form, and a Scandinavian name written with one letter does not map to the letter with a stroke.
sections.plainLanguage: Before 2003 there was no agreed way to put non-English letters in a domain name. IDNA's answer is to do the conversion in the application, so that the DNS servers and resolvers keep working with plain ASCII and nothing else has to be upgraded.

sections.title: Internationalized Labels and the ACE Prefix
sections.content:
A label is one part of a domain name, the pieces separated by dots. An internationalized label is a label that the ToASCII operation can process without failing. Because plain ASCII labels qualify, every ASCII domain name is also an internationalized domain name, and the term generalizes the old one rather than replacing it.

To let an internationalized label travel through protocols that only accept ASCII, IDNA defines an ACE label, short for ASCII Compatible Encoding. An ACE label is an internationalized label rendered in ASCII that is equivalent to a label that cannot be rendered in ASCII. An ACE label always begins with the ACE prefix, which is xn-- or any capitalization of it. The RFC gives xn--de-jg4avhby1noc0d as an example, where the part after the prefix is what the Punycode encoding produces.

Not every label that starts with the prefix is an ACE label, and the RFC says such labels should not be allowed in DNS zones because they confuse users. Two labels are treated as the same when their ASCII forms match, ignoring case, which extends the old rule that upper case and lower case are equivalent in ASCII names.
sections.plainLanguage: A label is one piece of a domain name, such as the word example in www.example.com. When a label contains non-ASCII characters, the application writes it in ASCII and marks it with the prefix xn-- so that other software can tell the difference between a genuine ASCII label and a converted one.

sections.title: The ToASCII Operation
sections.content:
ToASCII takes one label, a sequence of Unicode code points, and returns either a sequence of ASCII code points or a failure. If it succeeds, the input and the output are equivalent labels. It never changes a label that was already ASCII, and applying it more than once has the same effect as applying it once.

The operation has eight steps. If the label contains anything outside the ASCII range 0..7F, step 2 runs the Nameprep steps, which come from a profile of Stringprep, and fails on any error. If the UseSTD3ASCIIRules flag is set, step 3 checks that no code point outside letters, digits and hyphen is present and that the label does not begin or end with a hyphen. Step 5 then verifies that the label does not already begin with the ACE prefix, step 6 encodes the label with Punycode, step 7 prepends the prefix, and step 8 checks that the result holds between 1 and 63 code points.

ToASCII can fail, and the RFC is explicit about the consequence: if any step fails on any label of a domain name, that name must not be used as an internationalized domain name, and the application decides what to do about it. Implementations must fully implement Nameprep and Punycode; neither is optional.
sections.plainLanguage: ToASCII is the conversion that turns a label with non-ASCII characters into an ordinary ASCII label. It first normalizes the text, then encodes it with Punycode, then adds the xn-- prefix, and finally checks that the result is a legal label of at most 63 characters. If any step fails, the whole domain name is unusable as an internationalized name.

sections.title: The ToUnicode Operation
sections.content:
ToUnicode is the reverse conversion, used when a name is shown to a user. It takes a label and returns Unicode code points. If the input is an ACE label, the result is the equivalent internationalized label that is not in ACE form; otherwise the input is returned unaltered.

ToUnicode never fails. If a step fails, the original input is returned at that point. The output never contains more code points than the input. The steps are: skip ahead if the label is already ASCII, run Nameprep, confirm the label begins with the ACE prefix and keep a copy of it, remove the prefix, decode with Punycode and keep a copy of the result, run ToASCII on what was decoded, and check that the result matches the saved copy, ignoring case. Only then is the decoded copy returned.

The final check is what makes the operation safe to run on any input. A label that merely looks like an ACE label but does not decode to a matching label is left alone. The RFC notes that this means a name that still begins with the prefix after ToUnicode has run is not a valid ACE label and is not equivalent to any of the intermediate strings the operation built.
sections.plainLanguage: ToUnicode turns an xn-- label back into the characters a person would expect to see. It never fails: if anything goes wrong it hands back the label unchanged. That makes it safe to run on every name that comes out of the DNS, even names that only look like converted labels.

sections.title: How Applications and DNS Servers Use It
sections.content:
The RFC draws the arrangement as a stack. The user types and reads names at the top, the application does the ToASCII and ToUnicode work, and below it sit the resolver library and the DNS servers, which only ever see ACE labels. With a DNS resolver library, IDNA sits as a shim between the application and the library, so the library keeps its existing ASCII-only interface.

The requirements follow from that arrangement. Four things must hold: the characters U+002E, U+3002, U+FF0E and U+FF61 must all be recognized as label separators; a name put into a slot that does not understand internationalized names must contain only ASCII; an ACE label should be hidden from the user when the environment can show the non-ACE form; and two labels match if and only if their ASCII forms match, ignoring case.

Existing DNS servers need no change because every route into a server's database, such as master files and update messages, predates IDNA and is ASCII-only. The RFC states that there must be only one ASCII encoding for a given name, and the design of the two operations guarantees it. For DNSSEC, the ASCII form is the one that is signed, because the conversion happens before the zone is signed. The RFC also notes the cost: internationalized names are longer, so root servers carry a little more traffic and more queries may have to go over TCP rather than UDP.
sections.plainLanguage: The application sits between the user and the DNS. It converts what the user types before calling the resolver, and converts names coming back before showing them. The resolver and the DNS servers never see anything but ASCII. The price is length: converted names are longer, so there is slightly more traffic and some lookups move from UDP to TCP.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC starts from the fact that much of the Internet's security rests on the DNS. The encoding process itself introduces no new security issues beyond those of the ACE encoding, since it does not lengthen strings in a way that matters or allow new values.

The real risk is that two systems read the same internationalized name differently and send the user to different servers. The RFC leaves transcoding from a local character set to Unicode to the application, so two applications that implement different transcoding rules can disagree about the same name. It notes that protocols such as TLS do not solve this, because they do not take local character sets into account.

For that reason the RFC asks implementations to show a visual indication when a domain name mixes several scripts, so that a user can notice a name that contains both simplified and traditional Chinese characters or that confuses zero and one with the letters O and l. It also warns that any existing label starting with the ACE prefix that ToUnicode would alter becomes an ACE label automatically, whether or not the zone administrator intended that, and that implementations must not use a newer normalization table than the one this document references.
sections.plainLanguage: The risk is not the encoding but disagreement about it. If two programs read the same non-English name differently, a user can be sent to the wrong server, and TLS will not catch that. The RFC therefore asks programs to point out names that mix scripts, and it fixes one version of the normalization table so that everyone maps the characters the same way.

viz.caption: THE STEPS OF THE ToASCII OPERATION (RFC 3490)

items.label: SKIP IF ASCII
items.desc: If every code point is in the ASCII range 0..7F, go to step 3.

items.label: NAMEPREP
items.desc: Run the Nameprep steps on the label and fail on any error.

items.label: STD3 CHECKS
items.desc: If UseSTD3ASCIIRules is set, reject code points outside letters, digits and hyphen, and reject a leading or trailing hyphen.

items.label: SKIP IF ASCII
items.desc: If every code point is still in the ASCII range, go to step 8.

items.label: NO ACE PREFIX
items.desc: Verify that the label does not begin with the ACE prefix.

items.label: PUNYCODE
items.desc: Encode the label with Punycode and fail on any error.

items.label: LENGTH CHECK
items.desc: Verify that the label holds between 1 and 63 code points.
